prompt.context: Your company is a rather successful producer of candy. It originally started as a single product company and has diversified its product line over the last few years. The production process consists of two basic activities: manufacturing and packaging. The firm has also expanded its sales through product line extensions.
prompt.question: Management is concerned that sales are growing, but profits are not increasing at the same rate. What can your company do?

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to raw material costs?
clarifying_info.a: Raw materials are commodities with cyclical prices, which have fallen in recent years but are expected to swing up again.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to labor and fixed capital costs?
clarifying_info.a: Labor and fixed capital has increased per unit over-proportionally compared with ten years ago.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the cost explosion occurring — manufacturing or packaging?
clarifying_info.a: The cost explosion occurs in packaging. The product line extension is primarily an issue of different packaging; candy itself is largely the same product.

clarifying_info.q: How is the company's controlling/scheduling system set up?
clarifying_info.a: The controlling system still focuses on the manufacturing part of production. Packaging is not scheduled or controlled, causing slack in labor and fixed capital — small batch sizes and high setup times.

clarifying_info.q: What is the nature of the company's customers and retail relationships?
clarifying_info.a: There is concentration among retailers. Retailers demand large introductory discounts for new products, and new products have a high failure rate. Trade (private-label) brands also compete for shelf space.

framework: Revenue vs. cost analysis: sales growing but profits lagging — margins are shrinking
Decompose costs: raw materials (commodity/cyclical), labor, fixed capital
Identify where cost overruns occur: manufacturing vs. packaging
Assess revenue-side pressures: retailer concentration, trade brands, new product discounts and failure rates
Develop solutions to reduce costs and/or improve margins: scheduling, product line rationalization, marketing mix

questions.prompt: Where in the production process is the primary cost problem, and why?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that manufacturing is already efficiently controlled, whereas packaging is uncontrolled — leading to small batch sizes and high setup times. The product line extension manifests as many different packaging formats rather than fundamentally different candy products, so packaging is where the slack accumulates.

questions.prompt: What are the key revenue-side pressures the company faces?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) retailer concentration giving buyers pricing power; (2) trade/private-label brands competing on shelf; (3) retailers demanding large introductory discounts for new products; (4) high failure rate of new product introductions, meaning most launch investment is wasted.

questions.prompt: What solutions would you recommend to improve profitability?
questions.guidance: Cost side: introduce controlling and scheduling for packaging (reduce setup times, increase batch sizes, eliminate slack in labor and fixed capital). Revenue/margin side: streamline/reduce the product line to cut low-margin SKUs; reduce the rate of new product introductions to limit wasted launch investment and retailer discount exposure; reduce or eliminate low-margin trade brand production; shift to pull marketing to reduce dependence on retailer promotional discounts. Qualifier: assess whether key retail customers will accept a reduced product line before committing to rationalization.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional revenue killers or cost drivers might the company investigate?

categories.name: Revenue killers
ideas: Retailer concentration — fewer, more powerful buyers
Large introductory discounts demanded by retailers for new SKUs
High new product failure rate — most launch investment not recovered

categories.name: Cost drivers
ideas: Commodity raw material prices expected to cycle back up
Uncontrolled packaging operations — small batches, high setup times
Over-proportional growth in labor and fixed capital per unit vs. 10 years ago
Proliferation of packaging variants driven by product line extensions

categories.name: Operational levers
ideas: Introduce scheduling and controlling for packaging
Consolidate packaging runs to increase batch sizes
Cross-train labor between manufacturing and packaging to reduce slack

recommendation: Introduce formal scheduling and cost control for the packaging operation to eliminate small-batch inefficiencies and reduce setup times
Rationalize the product line by eliminating low-margin SKUs and reducing the pace of new product introductions to lower retailer discount costs and wasted launch investment
Reduce or exit low-margin trade brand production to improve overall mix
Shift marketing investment toward pull strategies to reduce dependence on retailer-demanded promotional discounts
risks: Key retail customers may be unwilling to accept a reduced product line, risking shelf-space loss
Raw material commodity prices are expected to rise, further compressing margins if cost actions are insufficient
Cutting new products too aggressively could slow long-term revenue growth
next_steps: Conduct retailer interviews to gauge acceptance of SKU rationalization
Build SKU-level profitability analysis to identify lowest-margin products
Benchmark packaging scheduling practices against industry peers
Model impact of expected raw material price increases under current vs. optimized cost structure
